Ares and Blackstone turn private credit and buyout fee streams into dividends, with $90,000 across Ares, Blackstone and Carlyle producing about $3,389 annually.

Carlyle pays a fixed $1.40 annual dividend, covered by $1.12 in quarterly distributable earnings against a $0.35 payout.

Ares offers the top yield at about 4%, but third-quarter realized income of $1.26 per share fell short of its $1.35 payout.

Getting into a private equity or private credit fund usually takes millions of dollars and years of locked-up money. The firms that run those funds trade like any other stock, though, and they send a large share of their fee income to shareholders as dividends. The three managers below manage about $2.52 trillion combined, using third-quarter figures from Carlyle and Ares and second-quarter figures for Blackstone.

Private equity means buying whole companies, improving them, and selling them years later. Private credit means lending directly to businesses without a bank or bond market in the middle. Managers collect steady management fees on the money they manage, plus performance fees when deals pay off. Fee-related earnings are the profit from those recurring fees alone, before any deal gains.

A $30,000 investment in each of these three high-yield names would produce the following income. Spread across all three, the $90,000 total produces $3,389 a year, using each company's latest quarterly dividend annualized. Prices are delayed quotes from the morning of Nov. 16, 2026, except Stock #3, which uses its Nov. 13 close.

Carlyle runs buyout funds, a global credit arm with $207 billion in assets, and AlpInvest, which buys fund stakes secondhand. Total assets under management were $479 billion at the end of the third quarter. Its fee business needs little capital, so most cash can go back to shareholders. Carlyle currently pays a fixed $1.40 a year, or $0.35 a quarter.

Third-quarter distributable earnings, the cash profit these firms use to set payouts, came to $1.12 per share against that $0.35 dividend. Carlyle also bought back 4.5 million shares in the quarter, with $1.4 billion left on its buyback authorization. Fewer deals to sell pose the biggest risk, as fee-related earnings fell to $292.6 million from $311.9 million a year earlier.

Blackstone ended the second quarter with a record $1.35 trillion in assets across real estate, private equity, credit and insurance, and hedge fund solutions. Its credit platform alone held nearly $550 billion. The dividend equals about 85% of Blackstone's share of distributable earnings, so it changes every quarter and the income figure is an estimate. The latest payout was $1.12, while the highest of the last four was $1.49.

In the second quarter, distributable earnings of $1.52 per share covered a $1.29 dividend, and fee-related earnings grew 22%. Michael Chae, chief financial officer on the July 23 call, described the policy as "basically returning 100% over time of our cash earnings back in the form of our dividend." The risk lies with individual investors: redemption requests at BCRED, its private credit fund for wealthy clients, topped the 5% limit. Separately, Australia's IDP rejected Blackstone's third buyout attempt, Reuters reported.

Ares leans hardest into private credit, managing $690.6 billion as of Sept. 30, 2026, with its Credit Group as the largest part. Private credit has grown as companies seek lenders who can move faster than banks, and 83% of Ares' credit debt assets float with interest rates, which raises fund returns and fees when rates rise.

The $1.35 quarterly dividend rose over 20% from a year ago. Coverage is tighter here: third-quarter after-tax realized income was $1.26 per share, below the payout, though year-to-date it reached $3.79. Capital not yet making fees could add about $826.9 million in annual management fees. Credit losses are the key risk, with U.S. direct lending nonaccruals at 1.8%.

Three Fee Streams, One Income Total

These 3 positions together generate $3,389 in annual passive income on a $90,000 investment, a combined yield of 3.77%. Ares contributes $1,203, Blackstone adds $1,130, and Carlyle rounds out the group with $1,056.

Owning the managers lets everyday investors share in the fees that wealthy clients pay to get into private funds, and the shares can be sold on any trading day. The payouts still rise and fall with the deal cycle, so Blackstone's estimate and Ares' coverage are worth checking each quarter.
